tldr: A multi-faceted study reveals that while the general-purpose foundation model GPT-6-Astra exhibits astonishing performance in robot control, major hurdles remain before reaching practical intelligence in the real world.
hero_caption: Performance comparison of GPT-6-Astra across 12 robotics benchmarks. By using in-context learning (ICL) from demonstrations and substantially increasing execution steps, it significantly outperforms existing SOTA and agent methods on many tasks, reaching near-saturation scores.
overview:
With the rapid advancement of large language and multimodal models, a central question has emerged among researchers: Can a general-purpose model directly control a robot body? In conventional robotics, training specialized policies (such as VLAs or world action models) for individual tasks and hardware embodiments has been standard practice. However, the arrival of GPT-6-Astra, a cutting-edge frontier model, is beginning to challenge that premise.

To investigate this, the authors devised an evaluation protocol that freezes GPT-6-Astra's weights entirely, leverages in-context learning (ICL) by including task demonstration videos in the prompt, and significantly expands execution steps to allow retries upon failure. Evaluating this setup across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile manipulators, dexterous hands, and navigation, the model demonstrated remarkable adaptability, substantially outperforming existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) records across many metrics.

Yet the story does not end there. A deeper look reveals that these high success rates depend on favorable assumptions: simulators pause time during inference, and there are no penalties for dangerous collisions or hardware damage. Through experiments across 8 real robot configurations and a prototype next-generation home benchmark where time never stops and evaluation is based on practical outcome utility, a reality far from practical embodied intelligence became evident: agents fall behind due to slow inference latency, fail to recover from irreversible mistakes (like spilled liquids or dropped parts), and lack awareness of their own physical dimensions.
contributions: Comprehensively evaluated the limit performance of GPT-6-Astra across 12 benchmarks under a unified protocol combining weight-frozen in-context learning (ICL) with substantially expanded execution steps.

Systematically analyzed coordination protocols between high-level System 2 reasoning and low-level System 1 control, as well as the impact of action representations and chunking designs on performance and inference cost.

Deployed zero-shot policies across 8 real-world hardware platforms—including single-arm, bimanual, dexterous hands, mobile bases, and humanoids—revealing real-world-specific constraints and behaviors.

Proposed core principles for next-generation embodied benchmarks centered on running world clocks, zero in-domain demonstrations, and real human utility, constructing an empirical prototype in Isaac Sim.

sections.heading: Will General-Purpose Models Make Specialized Roboticists Obsolete?
sections.summary: Prompted by GPT-6-Astra's impressive competence in robot control, this study re-examines its achievements, limitations, real-world deployment gaps, and future evaluation standards through four pillars: simulation, control harness design, real-robot experiments, and next-generation benchmarks.
sections.details:
Robotics learning has traditionally centered on training specialized policies from demonstration data collected specifically for individual tasks and hardware configurations. However, frontier models like GPT-6-Astra are beginning to display zero-shot generalization without weight updates, learning on the fly from in-context prompts and recovering from failures. This raises a fundamental question: Is this general-purpose model truly smart enough to render traditional specialized models obsolete?

Using GPT-6-Astra as a lens, this report explores where the field of embodied intelligence should head next. First, keeping the model's weights frozen, the authors evaluated it under an in-context learning (ICL) setup that grants access to the same demonstration information used by learning-based methods, alongside a substantially relaxed step limit. Under this protocol, the model achieved outstanding scores that surpassed existing methods and brought many tasks close to saturation.

However, these results cannot be celebrated uncritically. Closer analysis reveals severe vulnerabilities: massive inference costs and execution times, visual misidentification of physical success criteria, and an inability to recover from irreversible failures. Furthermore, real-world robot deployments and tests on a new, reality-grounded benchmark highlight a substantial gap between existing evaluation metrics and practical embodied intelligence.

sections.heading: Unified Evaluation Reveals GPT-6-Astra's Incredible Ceiling and Hidden Limits
sections.summary: Across 12 benchmarks, GPT-6-Astra was evaluated using demonstration-derived knowledge packages and a 10× increase in trial steps. While it achieved overwhelming success rates above 90% in many environments, failure modes like poor out-of-distribution transfer and physical verification errors also came to light.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Evaluation Protocol Design
Conventional trained policies learn from benchmark training sets, making a comparison without demonstrations unfair. Therefore, the authors adopted in-context learning (ICL), having GPT-6-Astra pre-analyze training demonstrations to generate "knowledge packages"—containing code, strategies, and reference trajectories—that it references at test time. Additionally, to allow the model to detect failures and execute recovery behaviors, they introduced a protocol extending the standard step budget ($1\times$) up to 10 times ($10\times$).

### 2.2 The Power of In-Context Learning
Under this framework, the results were striking. As shown in Fig. F1, success rates reached near-saturation above 98% on the LIBERO series and SIMPLE, and hit 87.3% on DexJoCo, a dexterous hand environment involving complex contacts. Knowledge packages automatically organize not just operational steps, but reference trajectories, visual references, executable helper functions for inverse kinematics, and success verification routines. In tasks where test setups closely match demonstration distributions, adapting these components yielded overwhelming performance.

### 2.3 The Impact of Extended Step Budgets
On high-precision bimanual and dexterous manipulation tasks (such as RoboDojo and Bench2Dex), where success rates hovered around 25% under standard steps ($1\times$), increasing the budget tenfold boosted success rates by 2 to 3 times. This gain stems from a functioning "self-correction loop," where the model detects intermediate mistakes and retries using alternative approaches.

### 2.4 Remaining Limits and Failure Modes
Nevertheless, major challenges persist. Typical failure cases are shown in Fig. F6:
- Generalization limits of knowledge packages: Performance drops sharply on tasks without demonstrations, exposing poor transferability.
- Cost and execution time: Difficult tasks in RoboDojo required several hours and millions of tokens for a single episode, far from practical viability.
- Physical-state verification errors: As shown in Fig. F6(a), the model often mistakes a hook merely overlapping a mug handle in the camera view for a successful hang, halting corrections even though the mug actually dropped onto the table.
- Inability to recover from irreversible failures: As seen in Fig. F6(b), when liquids spill or components drop to the floor, physical recovery is impossible, yet the model wastes steps continuing futile attempts.
- Destruction of long-horizon progress: As shown in Fig. F6(c), fine-tuning movements in later stages often undo earlier subgoals, such as accidentally knocking down headphones that had already been hung successfully.

captions.F1: Success rates of GPT-6-Astra + ICL across 12 benchmarks. Even under standard budgets (1×), it surpasses top existing methods, and extending steps to 10× achieves exceptional scores above 90% on LIBERO, SIMPLE, and DexJoCo.
captions.F6: Representative failure modes unresolved even with expanded steps: (a) visually misjudging contact or mating success, (b) failing to handle irreversible breakdowns like spilled liquid, and (c) destroying prior progress during later execution steps.

sections.heading: Connecting Brains to Limbs: Key Lessons in Control Harness Design
sections.summary: This section systematically compares coordination paradigms between high-level reasoning (GPT-6-Astra) and low-level control, along with action output representations. Closed-loop intervention and adaptive chunking are key to boosting success rates, though token consumption involves steep trade-offs.
sections.details:
Translating the core model's reasoning into physical robot movement heavily depends on the surrounding system architecture (the harness). The authors conducted ablation studies on 42 tasks from RoboDojo.

### 3.1 Coordination Between System 1 and System 2
The team compared ways to pair deep reasoning ("System 2", GPT-6-Astra) with fast low-level execution ("System 1", the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA model).
- Standalone VLA achieved only a 6.91% success rate, while open-loop coordination—where GPT simply supplies coarse subgoals—remained at 5.83%.
- In contrast, introducing a "closed-loop coordination" setup—where GPT pre-reviews, modifies, and approves end-effector (EEF) trajectories proposed by the VLA—improved success rates by more than 20 percentage points.
- However, reviewing every single action consumed roughly 7.66 million tokens. Grouping reviews into 4-action windows ($L=4$) cut token usage by 63.5% while slightly improving success to 25.83%. Combining this with ICL reached 54.17%, though at a massive cost of roughly 19.33 million tokens.

### 3.2 Action Representations and Action Chunking
The format of action commands issued by GPT-6-Astra is also critical.
- Directly predicting joint angles reduced success rates by 5.84 percentage points. There is a representational gap between the spatial reasoning of multimodal models and low-level joint space; semantic commands specifying relative end-effector translation and distance performed 2.50 percentage points higher.
- Furthermore, using "adaptive chunking"—allowing the model to dynamically choose execution horizons between 1 and 4 steps based on context rather than using fixed chunk sizes—yielded higher success rates (+4.44 percentage points) over fixed chunking.

sections.heading: Harsh Realities on Real Robots: Where Simulation Assumptions Break Down
sections.summary: GPT-6-Astra was evaluated zero-shot across 8 distinct hardware setups, including single-arm, bimanual, dexterous hands, mobile robots, and humanoids. While rigid-body picking proved robust, contact-rich manipulation, joint overheating, and lengthy inference latencies exposed unique real-world barriers.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Real-World Experimental Setup
The primary drivers of success in simulation were the availability of demonstrations and unlimited retry time. In the real world, however, demonstrations do not exist for unseen tasks, and trial-and-error directly risks hardware damage and safety hazards. Thus, real-robot experiments evaluated 8 hardware platforms under zero-shot conditions (no demonstrations), providing only prior human knowledge prompts (joint limits, gripper presets, etc.) and budgeting execution by real wall-clock time (typically 60 minutes) rather than execution steps.

### 4.2 Findings from Real-Robot Experiments
- A single model drives diverse hardware: As shown in Fig. F8, rigid-body tasks mirroring simulation—such as block stacking (6/6 success on Franka 3) and tape stacking—were executed with high accuracy. However, contact-rich tasks like cloth folding and plug insertion (0/11 combined across 3 platforms) proved exceptionally difficult.
- Emergence of active vision: Inserting a flower into a vase (Fig. F9) offers a clear example. With a single arm, the held flower occluded the vase opening, leading to failure. On a bimanual robot (Piper), the system maneuvered the camera on its free arm to look down into the vase opening before completing the insertion. This active viewpoint adjustment was not demonstrated in human teleoperation data; the model synthesized it independently to clear its line of sight.
- Controlling a humanoid robot (Unitree G1): By treating GPT-6-Astra as a slower System 2 supplying joint targets and walking velocities to a high-frequency walking controller (System 0), the setup successfully completed locomotion (3/3) and manipulation (2/3) trials.

### 4.3 Simulation Assumptions That Collapse in Reality
Unlike simulators, the premise of "just retry upon failure" fails on physical hardware.
- Safety constraints: Light contact with a table while tugging cloth triggered safety protective stops, abruptly terminating trials.
- Hardware limits: Repeated grasping attempts with dexterous hands caused actuator overheating, triggering safety shutdowns at 62°C. On the G1, the robot spent roughly 90% of its total time standing frozen awaiting inference, stretching a single trial past an hour. In the physical world, deliberation time itself creates hardware wear and operational risk.

captions.F8: Zero-shot control across 8 physical robot configurations. While rigid manipulation like block stacking is stable, tasks involving contact or spatial discrepancies—such as dexterous grasping or pushing washing machine buttons—required human guidance or replanning.
captions.F9: Active vision deciding task success. (a) With a single arm, the wrist camera is occluded by the flower, obscuring the vase opening and causing failure. (b) With bimanual arms, the free arm's camera moves to gain visual line of sight into the opening, achieving successful insertion.

sections.heading: As Robots Get Smarter, We Must Completely Redesign the Benchmarks
sections.summary: The authors propose three benchmark principles overturning legacy assumptions: human-need-driven tasks, autonomous exploration without demonstrations, and running world clocks. In an Isaac Sim household prototype, delays during reasoning caused new failure modes, such as burnt fried eggs.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Three Principles for Next-Generation Benchmarks
Most existing benchmarks are reverse-engineered from current robot capabilities, testing logical final states in frozen worlds. This fails to measure practical intelligence. The authors propose three new principles:
1. Human-needs-based task design: Specify goals via natural human requests like "make breakfast," scoring them on practical outcome utility (user satisfaction) rather than rigid target states. Crucially, implicit obligations (Duties)—such as closing the refrigerator door after use—are also graded.
2. Autonomous test-time experience acquisition: Provide zero prior demonstrations, requiring agents to discover unfamiliar household layouts and appliance mechanisms through their own exploration.
3. Running world clocks (real-time dynamics): The simulator clock keeps ticking while the model deliberates. If reasoning is slow, food on the stove will burn.

### 5.2 Household Prototype Demonstration
Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim, the authors built a 1LDK apartment environment featuring high-fidelity physics across fluids, rigid bodies, cloth, and thermal processes (Fig. F11). Zero-shot evaluation of GPT-6-Astra in this environment exposed revealing failures (Fig. F12):
- Tunnel vision causing collateral damage: While cleaning up a book, the robot's elbow shoved a monitor off a desk; after putting milk in the fridge, it left the door wide open for over 450 seconds.
- Neglecting physical embodiment: After opening the refrigerator door, the robot blocked its own path, repeatedly failing to reach bacon inside and letting the door swing shut.
- Worlds moving ahead during deliberation: As shown in Fig. F12(e), the agent correctly decided to turn off the stove after seeing an egg fry. However, processing images and generating actions took tens of seconds, leaving the egg completely charred before the burner was switched off.

### 5.3 Hurdles to Implementation
Scaling such real-time, high-fidelity benchmarks requires overcoming significant technical hurdles, including physical simulation accuracy, computational costs proportional to deliberation time, and building fair automated judges.

captions.F11: Pipeline for building next-generation household benchmarks. Combining open assets and physical bindings, the robot relies solely on onboard cameras to fulfill ambiguous human needs in a world where time never stops during deliberation.
captions.F12: Failure cases in the continuous-time household prototype: (a) collisions knocking items off desks, (b) duty violations leaving refrigerators open, (c) self-occlusion where the robot's body blocks food retrieval, and (e) burnt fried eggs caused by deliberation delays.

sections.heading: Beyond Saturated Benchmarks: Toward True Practical Embodied Intelligence
sections.summary: GPT-6-Astra marks a dramatic leap forward in embodied capabilities, but that does not mean practical intelligence is solved. The field must move away from chasing scores on isolated benchmarks toward engineering systems that operate safely and efficiently under real-world constraints.
sections.details:
The overarching conclusion from evaluating GPT-6-Astra is clear: embodied control using general-purpose models has taken a massive leap, but remains far from the finish line of practical embodied intelligence.

With in-context learning and extended trial budgets, many existing isolated benchmarks can now be saturated. However, the real problems we must solve have shifted elsewhere: cross-task generalization, long-horizon plan preservation, risk management to avoid irreversible mistakes, and above all, strict real-world constraints around time, cost, and hardware safety.

High benchmark scores do not translate directly into real-world deployability. Future robotics and AI research must look beyond competing solely on task success rates, entering a new frontier focused on building reliable systems that operate within physical hardware and temporal limits to meet real deployment demands.

sections.heading: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: VLAs, World Models, and Agentic Control
sections.summary: This section traces the evolution from LLM-based high-level planning to VLAs and world action models (WAMs) to contextualize the paper's contributions, surveying research on agent harnesses that convert reasoning into physical control.
sections.details:
This study builds upon the rapid convergence of robotics and foundation models in recent years.

### 8.1 Foundation Models as Embodied Agents
Early works (such as SayCan, Inner Monologue, and Code as Policies) used LLMs as high-level planners deciding "what to do," delegating low-level execution to pre-existing skill libraries or motion planners. In contrast, this paper investigates whether a frontier model can directly participate in the feedback loop to command end-effector actions. It also systematically analyzes the "harness"—infrastructure inspired by coding agents—by isolating its individual components.

### 8.2 The Evolution of Robot Policy Learning
Policy learning originated in imitation learning and recently advanced into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (such as OpenVLA and the $\pi$ series), bringing large-scale pretraining to robot control. More recently, World Action Models (WAMs) unifying video prediction with action generation have driven rapid progress. Rather than training specialized models from scratch, this paper takes a complementary stance, probing how effectively general-purpose models can serve as direct policies and how they can leverage VLAs as tools.

### 8.3 Evolution of Benchmarks and Empirical Studies
A variety of benchmarks exist, including LIBERO, RoboDojo, and BEHAVIOR, but most were designed to evaluate imitation learning policies. This study evaluates these suites under a single unified protocol while highlighting the urgent need for next-generation benchmarks that reflect an ongoing, dynamic real world.

takeaways: Without updating weights, general-purpose frontier models can match or outperform specialized models (VLAs/WAMs) given proper prompt engineering (ICL) and sufficient execution steps.
Rather than delegating control entirely to low-level controllers, a harness where System 2 (LLM) monitors and modifies end-effector trajectories in a closed loop is highly effective.
High simulation success relies on artificial assumptions—inference pausing world time and an absence of safety shutdowns—which do not directly translate into real-robot reliability.

Embodied AI evaluation must move away from static completion checks toward continuous environments where time ticks during reasoning, grading agents on real human needs and implicit duties like tidying up.
limitations: Inference can require several hours and millions of tokens per episode, making latency and computational costs prohibitive for commercial, real-time deployment.
When irreversible physical changes occur—such as spilled liquids or dropped components—the agent gets trapped in futile retry loops without realizing recovery is impossible.
In physical robot trials, the model cannot autonomously anticipate or manage hardware protection shutdowns, such as motor overheating in dexterous hands or emergency stops caused by contact forces.
